This brings the issue of how the observed values can be classiﬁed and whether the next set of observations can be accurately predicted. With the exponential rate of evolution of supervised learning algorithms, it is now possible to eﬃ- ciently and eﬀectively collect, store, process and analyze high volumes of data on parallel architectures, allowing for high accuracy predictions whilst keeping computation time short. The aim of this project is to discuss the viability of introducing machine learning models into navigation technologies, supported by a thorough development of such a model. The project also aims to compare popular classiﬁers to benchmark their performance, also oﬀering a short discussion of the suitability of the models for deployment into a live system. devices supported by machine learning plays an important role in data driven decision making - such a model has the ability to provide predic- tions in real time, based on real, accurate and live data. The ability to reliably predict future values based on some observed samples is possibly one of the most exciting challenges within the ﬁeld of machine learning. When applied on time series data, problems are classiﬁed as forecasting and time series analysis problems, where the goal is to predict the value of some observable variable y at time t or the value of t at which y = x. Classiﬁers are a category of supervised learning algorithms [17] which build a mathematical model of a supplied data set Y to make predictions ˆy in the future by ﬁnding some function f . The other category is regression, which is unfortunately out of the scope for this project, despite time series also being suitable for regressors in certain cases like predicting air pollution [15, 13] or rainfall [33]. A built model will unveil relationships in the data to make the pre- dictions; generally, the more accurate the data is, the stronger the predictions will be. In many cases, some form of feature engineering is essential as part of pre-processing, otherwise classiﬁers may ﬁnd false relations in the data. Supervised learning algorithms have typically been used for weather forecasting [84], stock market [62] and in medicine [89]. The quick execution time of such models are usable through cloud technologies [65] , which makes their use very lucrative to most sectors. Whilst popular map applications started including public transport timetables and road traﬃc information since 2007 [102], rail crossings are not recognised as an obstacle or a delay to a journey despite the crossings having the potential of signiﬁcantly aﬀecting one’s overall travel time. Including rail traﬃc information in map applications could help to foresee the traﬃc ahead (e.g. at upcoming level crossings), estimate the extra time for the journey and then issue reroutes in time if needed. 4 This paper places the focus on using classiﬁcation techniques on time series data to produce a model which can predict rail traﬃc, that could theoretically be implemented in a real time navigation application. It explains the production of a multi-class classiﬁer which answers the question ”is the crossing traversable at t?; if not, how long for?”. By being able to answer for current time t, it can also be answered for t + 1, t + 2, ..., t + k as well, hence being able to provide a forecast to some degree. The paper can be used as a guide for solving a time series based classiﬁcation problem in general, as the methods outlined here can rigorously be applied to other problems where some event E happens at time t, or the value y of something is x at time t. Before diving straight into the method, Chapter 2 outlines preliminary knowl- edge that is required for understanding the developed method - the idea behind classiﬁers which are explored as well as some techniques that are applied dur- ing data preparation. Chapter 3 describes the motivation and the execution of building such a classiﬁer step by step, pointing out ways of improvement at times. The results achieved by the method are then described and assessed in Chapter 4, also oﬀering a discussion of the obtained results and ways to improve the model(s) further. Chapter 5 then argues the strongest and most suitable model along with some additional statistics based on the collected data. 5 Chapter 2 Prerequisite understanding It is essential to ﬁrst lay down preliminary knowledge of the techniques and algorithms used, their eﬀectiveness and reason for their use. The classiﬁers dis- cussed in this chapter have been selected to build a model for the purpose of this project. In general, one should try multiple classiﬁers - usually with several set of hyperparameters - to ultimately come up with one that works the best according to the selected metric(s). In some cases, it is not possible to increase a classiﬁer’s eﬀectiveness without changing the data structure [50]; in most in- stances, the best model is discovered by trying diﬀerent sets of hyperparameters [10, 9]. To evaluate a model eﬀectively, forms of cross validation [86] should be employed, also covered in this chapter. 2.1 Nearest Neighbour Nearest neighbour operates on the logic that when data points are plotted, those belonging to the same class are likely to be near each other [35]. It assigns the class label to a test sample based on its k neighbours [69, 3]. If k = 1, the test sample is assigned the class of the absolute nearest neighbour, and for k > 1 the majority class of the k nearest neighbours is assigned. Let there be n training samples, each with features m and a classiﬁcation la- bel of the sample c, s = [x0, x1, ..., xm, c]. Let the objective function be the Euclidean distance d(x, s) = √(X1 − S1)2 + (X2 − S2)2. If a test sample is x and the training samples are S = {s0, s1, ..., sn} then we calculate d(x, s) for each s ∈ S, and sort the results in ascending order. Take the ﬁrst k classiﬁcation labels, c, and assign to x the most common value of c [95]. Example. It is beneﬁ- cial to monitor the chosen metric values over several odd values of k, identify 8 where the classiﬁer’s accuracy starts dropping and choose the suitable value accordingly. 2.2 Random Forest Random forest works by constructing many decision trees that each make their individual predictions, carry out majority voting and the input is then classiﬁed by the label that has the most votes [14]. Bootstrap aggregation, or bagging, is a concept where a random number of samples are selected from the original set with replacement, making the trees correlate less - the trees need to correlate with each other as little as possible [78] so that each tree behaves diﬀerently and thus increasing the accuracy [21]. Algorithm 1 Growing a random forest Considering N as the number of training samples, Tb a tree, m the number of chosen features out of total p features, the algorithm to grow a forest of many trees in general is: 1. Draw a bootstrap sample of size N 2. Grow a tree on the bootstrapped data, by recursively carrying out the operations for each node of the tree until a stopping condition is met (e.g. minimum node size): (a) Select m random variables (b) Pick the best variables among m to split via Gain(S, F ) (c) Split the node into two daughter nodes (unless pure) 3. Output all trees of the forest In the following subsections, the algorithm is explored more in-depth, consider- ing the available hyperparameters and their eﬀect on the overall performance. 2.2.1 Hyperparameters In general, hyperparameters all have lower and upper bounds, outside of which they start negatively aﬀecting the performance of the forest [78]. There are several hyperparameters that could either inﬂuence the complexity of a forest, serve as a stopping condition or impact accuracy. Consider those with the biggest impact on performance [60, 78]: 1. n-estimators - the number of decision trees constructed, 2. max-features - the number of features to be considered while deciding a split, 9 3. max-depth - the number of levels a tree is allowed to have, 4. min-samples-split - deﬁning how many samples a node must contain before it can be split, 5. min-samples-leaf - deﬁning the number of samples a leaf node must have at least This is the list of the most commonly adjusted parameters, which all have the largest eﬀect on the accuracy of a model. n-estimators. The number of decision trees used for the voting process. The more trees there are, the more accurate a model becomes as stated by Liaw & Wiener [63], but high values are computionally expensive, making the building process slow. 1 max-features. Increasing this value may also increase the performance of the model, because it can now select more features to split from [78]. However, it also makes the trees less diverse; intuitively, lowering this value means that the trees will correlate less and produce more stable results [78] which may be worse on average than with a higher value [78]. It is then essential to ﬁnd the optimal value that neither under nor overﬁts the model. By default, packages typically use √p [75] where p is the number of total features. max-depth. When a tree makes a large number of splits (and therefore has a large depth), it has the potential to explain the variation of the data, but this may also result in overﬁtting. Note that in certain cases, this parameter should be untouched so that trees can make splits until their leaves are pure, 2 as intended. min-samples-split. Deﬁning the number of samples required for a split can be very bad for a model, because there is the potential that nodes do not achieve purity due to insuﬃcient samples (and thus splits). This value therefore should be based on the size of the training data set [78]. min-samples-leaf. Similarly to the previous parameter, large values can cause a setback for the model rather than the opposite. With too high of a value, the trees may not be able to capture suﬃcient patterns within the data due to being unable to split enough times [78]. This therefore depends on the size of the training set and requires tuning [78]. 2.2.2 Measuring the quality of a split Decision trees are constructed such that the most signiﬁcantly separating fea- tures and decisions are at the top of the tree - in other words, information gain is computed for each feature and the one yielding the best value is picked ﬁrst. The information gain of each remaining feature is computed again, choosing the highest value which determines the most signiﬁcant split. This is a supervised learning algorithm that learns a function f (·) : Rm ↦→ Ro by training [41], where m is the number of features in the input vector and o is the output dimension. An ANN consists of multiple layers: input, hidden layer(s) and an output. In each hidden layer, there are r neurons that carry out the calculations (note that r might be diﬀerent for each hidden layer), whereas in the input and output layer there are typically one neuron each 3. The input layer takes in n inputs of x, each with m features, x = [x1, x2, ..., xm]. The hidden layer transforms the values from the previous layer with a weighted linear summation, immediately followed by some non-linear activation function σ(x) [22]. Several hidden layers may follow each other immediately, however a maximum of two are usually more than enough for a task [49]. The output layer is the evaluated prediction ˆy, an n × 1 column vector, which has one output for each vector of x regardless the number of its features. Consider the simple network depicted by Figure 2.3. Figure 2.6: Simple Neural Network with one hidden layer ... ... ... x1 x2 x3 xn H1 Hn ˆy1 ˆy2 ˆy3 ˆyn Input layer Hidden layer Ouput layer 3in the case of multi class classiﬁcation, for k classes there are k output neurons for each input xi ∈ x 16 2.3.1 Propagation The way ANNs make sense of the input is by having individual weight vectors W associated with each layer that weight each feature of the input. On the creation of a network, the entries of the weight vectors are by default random numbers on the interval [0, 1). The network needs to be trained to memorise the relationship(s) present in the data in order to make the future predictions. Note that there can be a single bias unit included in the input- and following hidden layers, which allows the ﬁtting of data even if all input values are 0 [44]. When some input x enters the network, the neurons in the current layer carry out a weighted linear summation with their individual weight vector W , described by x′ = x · W . Note that this is the same as x′ = x1 ∗ w1 + x2 ∗ w2 + ... + xm ∗ wm. Then, the activation function, σ(x′), processes the output of the layer and the value(s) are passed forward to the next layer which repeats this procedure. Therefore individual weight matrices are kept track of by, and are essentially attached to, each layer. There are many neurons that have their own weights for each layer - for r neurons, there are r weight matrices associated with each input n. Once the initial input reaches the end of the output layer, one propa- gation has been completed, at which point it needs to backpropagate to update the weights W relative to the error. 2.3.2 Backpropagation Let’s notate each weight vector, Wij as the link between layer i and j, similarly x′ i as the output of layer i and xi as the vectors in the layer. Once the ﬁrst propagation is ﬁnished, a loss function - in classiﬁcation’s case, Cross-Entropy [72] - is calculated, which in binary case is Loss(ˆy, y, W ) = −yln(ˆy) − (1 − y)ln(1 − ˆy) + α∥Wij∥ 2 2 where α∥Wij∥ 2 2 is an L2-regularization [32] (penalty) term. α > 0 is a non- negative hyperparameter controlling the magnitude of the penalty [74]. After the loss has been computed, it is propagated starting from the output layer backwards, updating each W on the way. The gradient ∆Loss ij W of the loss with respect to the weights Wij is computed and deducted from Wij: W ′ ij = Wij − η∆Loss ij W [38] where η > 0 is the learning rate. The repeated updates then minimise the loss function, thus converging to the most optimal relationship. The learning rate is deﬁned by the optimizer used, which in this case is simply the Adam [59] optimizer. 2.3.3 Training Once the network has propagated forwards and backwards once, it has done 1 epoch of training. Training worth of d epochs means that the inputs are 17 propagated through the network, the weights are updated and this is repeated another d − 1 times. Then the network is used on a test set to determine its performance according to some metric. By default [74], training is carried out for a speciﬁed number of iterations, or alternatively when the improvement in loss is below a certain, small threshold. 2.3.4 Activation function The activation function’s role in the model is to produce a non-linear signal for the next layer [22]. Considering that neurons calculate weighted linear sums, without an activation function each output signal is simply a linear function, which is easy to solve but limited in complexity; it would make the network a linear regression model[101]. There are a handful of non-linear functions σ(x) that are commonly used depending on the context of the problem [101]. It is possible - and often required - to use diﬀerent activation functions layer to layer. Sigmoid. The logistic function is on the interval [0, 1), described by σ(x) = 1 1 + e−x Its prediction ˆy ≤ 0.5 will belong to Class 0 and ˆy > 0.5 to Class 1. This activa- tion function is standard for binary classiﬁcation but there are some concerns. The function is not zero centered and has a slow convergence - these properties make the derivative of the function unstable, resulting in gradient updates going too far in either direction during backpropagation [101]. Hyperbolic tan. Given by σ(x) = 1 − e−2x 1 + e−2x , tanh(x) is on the interval [−1, 1]. The function is therefore zero centered, mak- ing the overall optimisation easier but still suﬀers from the vanishing gradient problem [101] whereby weights can die out. Rectiﬁed linear unit (ReLU). ReLU is proven to be more eﬀective than tanh because it does not suﬀer from the vanishing gradient problem [61, 108]. It is given by the simple function σ(x) = max(0, x). Whilst there is advice against using it in the output layer [108], some studies have experimented with using ReLU in place of sof tmax [1, 2, 4]. Generally, an advantage (and sometimes a disadvantage) is that this activation function can cause neurons to die where their weights become 0 [108, 90, 22]. Softmax. It is given by σ(x) = xi ∑J j=1 exj frequently used in multi-class classiﬁcation problems as the output layer activa- tion function [103, 56, 106] to calculate the probability of x belonging to each class. 18 ReLU as the default activation function in the hidden layer(s) [22], and sof tmax or sigmoid in the output layer [45] is a combination often recommended [90] for multi or binary class networks respectively. 2.4 One-hot encoding The concept of one-hot is an encoding technique that helps preparing data set for various Machine Learning algorithms, like classiﬁers and regression models [23]. In the world of mathematics and computer science, one often carries out mappings of text data to numerical, for example let m = {Jan, F eb, ..., Dec} and M = {1, 2, ..., 12} then f : m ↦→ M . It is natural to represent chronological data as such, especially when data is stored for later processing, but this can lead to algorithms learning non-existing or biased patterns in the data [68, 19]. Example. Let’s label and store days in a single feature, day, with its val- ues satisfying 1 ≤ day ≤ 7. Feeding this data in with several other columns of data may teach the algorithm that the relationship investigated is much more prevalent on Sundays, but that could be down to the simple fact that 7 is the biggest number in that feature. This division 19 is done by ﬁrst shuﬄing the data randomly, then taking a certain proportion (usually 10 or 20%) [86, 92] of all data and delegating it as the test set whilst the rest of the data is trained on. Once the classiﬁer is trained, its metrics are determined by using the model on the delegated test set and determining the proportion it gets right. Not only will this in itself not give a true metric of the data [46], but the potential of the data set is also being wasted by not all of it being used [46]. Therefore it is desired to use a cross validation technique, which uses the entire set of available data for both training and testing. There are diﬀerent approaches available like leave-one-out [98], but let’s focus on the simple n-fold [7] approach here: Algorithm 2 N-Fold cross validation 1. Divide the data set S into n even sized partitions 2. Iterate up to i = n 2.1. Take the partition at index i = 0 as the test set and remaining n − 1 partitions as training 2.2. Train a model on the training set and use the delegated test set to evaluate the model 2.3. Retain model metrics and discard the model 2.4. Repeat for next i 3. Take an average of the retained metrics to get a true score across the entire available data 4. Repeat process for a model with diﬀerent hyperparameters if required Values of n are chosen such that a partition is large enough to be statistically representative of the broader data set. Typical values are ∈ 5, 10 as these usually create large enough partitions. A higher value of n leads to a less biased model [88] (as all data points are being used) and helps avoid overﬁtting [88], but there might be a higher variation if there are any outliers in the set [99]. 20 Chapter 3 Method 3.1 Overview The goal of this project is to build a classiﬁer that is able to determine the state, S, of a train crossing at a random time t during a day d. To realize such a classiﬁer, there needs to be a time series data stream by the day, capturing the times of a level crossing barrier descending and ascending, and the length of this interval. The series needs to be broken down by the day, to account for the simple fact that traﬃc patterns change according to the day of the week as well as the time of the day. Therefore, an overarching classiﬁer must be able to diﬀerentiate between days of the week. The state S can simply be binary labels to indicate only the untraversability of a rail crossing (False when the barrier is ascended, and True for a descended position), or multiple classes that are assigned based on some other feature of the observations. Since the interest is in not only in the current state, but also in how long the state remains the same for, classes are assigned to each sample based on the length of the interval. This means that when predicting a state S, what is being predicted is how long the barrier is likely to be down for and not just whether it is currently untraversable or not. 3.2 Data Collection Possibly the most optimal way to capture a time series on the movement of a level crossing is using a Raspberry Pi, programmed to take and analyse real time video. The main and foremost prob- lem is that it is not possible to process the data set because there are columns of datetime objects, but algorithms can, natively, only deal with number data types. It is possible to carry out a simple transformation, converting the times- tamps into seconds (from midnight), but that in itself is not suﬃcient. The model would not be particularly good, because it would not know that the data is cyclic. Assume, that there is routinely a train 2 minutes after midnight. This means that the barrier will more than likely drop just before midnight (let’s say 23:59) and ascend sometime after midnight (00:05). Clearly the diﬀerence in time is 360 seconds, but in this form they will appear to be 23 hours and 54 27 minutes apart, and the connection will never be made [64]. Table 4.1 shows that this data set is quite unbalanced - observations of c4 are rare cases, which means that a model might perform poorly on this class according to some metric. It is therefore vital to understand the metrics available to be able to assess models according to vari- ous diﬀerent aspects. Accuracy, acc = T P +T N T otal , is the most natural but also misleading metric - it is misleading when the set is highly unbalanced [48, 53, 27]. Let’s consider an example of a total of 100 entries, 10 out of which belong to Class A and 90 belonging to Class B. In this case if the classiﬁer guesses Class B for each entry, it will achieve a 90% accuracy purely because of the distribution of examples. Precision is the fraction of relevant instances among the classiﬁed instances, or otherwise, the number of correctly identiﬁed samples within the given class, given by P r = T P T P +F P [53]. This metric becomes important when the model in question should absolutely make correct classiﬁcations [77]. In the case of this data set, the goal is to have a high value of precision for across all classes. This is important because it means that the classiﬁer can reliably classify entries and that when it classiﬁes an entry, the classiﬁcation is correct. Recall describes the number of correctly identiﬁed instances over the class size, or otherwise, Rc = T P T P +T N [53]. Let’s consider a simple example of a picture containing 15 dogs and some cats. Suppose a script identiﬁes 9 dogs in this pic- ture. Out of the identiﬁed 9 dogs, only 7 are actually dogs, while the remaining 2 are cats. The precision then is 7 9 and recall is 7 15 . Therefore a good model should have both a high precision and recall rate over high accuracy. F1-Score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall rate [77], F 1 = 2 P r∗Rc P r+Rc , insensitive to the distribution of the incorrect predictions over the classes [42]. The harmonic mean is a truer average than arithmetic or geometric average because it is always the least of the three [107]. It’s best value is at 1 which would mean a perfect precision and recall rate. For each of these metrics, there is a macro and micro metric available [93], which is mostly signiﬁcant for classiﬁcation problems with classes c > 2. In gen- eral, the macro version will compute the metric independently for each class and then take the average. Micro, on the other hand, computes a weighted average [8]. Micro averages are important for unbalanced data sets because the class imbalance is captured and thus the average performance remains high, even if there are no classiﬁcations of one class [80]. The models in this case are evaluated according to the macro average and weighted average of the f1-score. 33 4.1.2 Reducing sample size Each model will be trained using the available data set, as well as a reduced data set where classes are more balanced. Longer collection time. The data collection ran for 13 weeks, starting De- cember 2019 until March 2020, so running for longer could have improved the results. However, this was nearly impossible due to time constraints and the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic would have no doubt aﬀected the results since the 43 use of public transport heavily dropped [58, 71, 87, 39]. Collecting from other relevant locations. Collecting data for multiple rel- evant train stations increases the sample size. However data could not be used across stations, therefore an additional location feature would have to be intro- duced to create one overarching classiﬁer. There are no doubt other stations situated next to a level crossing as there are approximately 7500 level crossings in Great Britain [79]. In this case, the manual measurements taken at the level crossing situated next to the station of Lincoln Central might not be entirely accurate for similar crossings. Smaller class partitions. The classes for this problem are dependent on which interval the length feature falls in for the entry, but these are not placed at a uniform distance away as shown earlier. Therefore creating k classes, starting from length = 0 to length = max, each placed at an even distance i, might be a better model for predicting much better values. Even in this case, it is very likely that the data will be imbalanced, and thus some additional work may be needed to possibly drop some of the last classes and their observations completely. Overcoming class imbalance. One issue which has been mentioned a lot is that classes are severely imbalanced, even in the data sets which are undersam- pled; there are Near-Miss algorithms that use a Nearest Neighbour classiﬁer to select which samples to remove [66], amongst other intelligent undersampling methods [57]. Oversampling is similar, whereby random observations are du- plicated in the minority group [97] or in the case of images, transformed; e.g. rotated, translated or otherwise transformed, or picking out speciﬁc features [76]. Oversampling has been shown to run the risk of overﬁtting [28] and so any form of oversampling must be carried out methodically [26, 47, 25]. Better manual readings. Another simple performance increase may occur by having more accurate data for the manual measurements. This could include either more randomly sampled readings throughout the day or readings taken at deﬁned intervals every day. The latter might be better in the case that these values change throughout each day. Improved values will increase the eﬃciency of Algorithm 3 since with smaller tw there will be more, shorter sessions; td could be modelled by a more accurate distribution and tu would be a truer mean - all increasing the quality of the data. All of this could be improved if the data is collected directly on the crossing via template matching [24] or various tracking [31] methods. Concept of freight trains. As described by Table 4.1, there are not many observations of cases where the level crossing was untraversable for longer than 300 seconds - in those cases, it was usually due to trains bunching up with late trains and causing a delay. An interesting aspect to include in the algorithm would have been freight trains, which passing by are typically slow and long. There is no publicly available information on freight trains but one way could have been to artiﬁcially ”schedule” two freight trains [104] for a random time taken from an arbitrary time interval during a day. Better feature engineering. Previously described points could increase the quality of the data, but other techniques remain available in terms of prepro- 44 cessing. Perhaps the most signiﬁcant feature engineering technique that can be applied is the concept of larger shifts ⇓n - one could add additional ⇓n features for sina and cosa as well as |length| up until some arbitrary value which im- proves the model’s memory. This was not investigated here in depth beyond a lag feature of 1, because each diﬀerent model would have to be trained and cross validated individually, which takes on average 20-28 hours for each gener- ation. It may be that there is correlation between an upcoming value f (t) and an arbitrary κ number of previous values [85], but unfortunately this could not be tested. 45 Chapter 5 Conclusion This paper produces a structured and systematic method for building a multi class time series predictor, containing approaches, models and the logical steps. There were two classiﬁer models produced using each chosen supervised learning algorithm. Each learning algorithm was trained on the entire data set generated by the developed data simulating algorithm, and on a reduced, more balanced data set randomly sampled from the original data set to investigate the dif- ference in performance. These models were ranked according to two diﬀerent metrics, f1 macro average and f1 weighted average. All models were considered according to each metric, but ultimately the models are ranked in accordance with their macro average scores, because the goal of this classiﬁer is to recognise as many samples as possible across each class. The best performing classiﬁer was Random Forest trained on the reduced data set, with 65%; followed by the other Random Forest model with 58%. Interestingly Nearest Neighbour trained on the full data set only did 1% worse, also being a close second with 79% weighted average. The reduced Nearest Neighbour model is followed by the ANN model at 44% macro average, failing to recognise any observations from c4. The second ANN trained on the full data set performed 4% worse, also failing to recognise any c4 or c3 observations. Whilst the f1 scores were relatively low in general, it was demonstrated that with more data it is possible to produce a reliable classiﬁer which can predict level crossing clo- sures in real-time with this method. The performance was mostly lacking due to the unreliability and questionable integrity of the collected data; it was not possible to use sensors or a camera for data collection so the data quality could be improved, but good feature engineering is also vital. Other than increasing the data quality, some other techniques could have been used to exploit the full potential in the data, like multiple time shift features, more than four classes to try to balance data fur- ther or oversampling rare cases. These changes unfortunately turned to be out of scope due to the training times of 20-28 hours per model. 46 In general, the project has been a success despite ways of improvements remain- ing uninvestigated due to time constraints; one major setback for the project was the inability of using computer vision techniques for data collection, which would have been the equivalent of a sensor and there would not be a reliance on the created algorithm for the data stream.
